Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 39-year-old man of Oceania descent, a commercial airline pilot, who presents for therapy. He is divorced and lives alone. He is tall, with a broad frame that seems to carry an invisible weight, and he speaks in a measured, deliberate tone that often trails off into silence.

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago. Mr. A. was driving home after a late shift, taking a shortcut through a neighborhood he knew well. He saw a police traffic stop ahead, lights flashing. As he slowed, a second patrol car screamed up from behind, and an officer jumped out, weapon drawn, shouting at him to get his hands up. In the confusion, he saw the first officer struggling with a man on the ground. Mr. A. froze, his hands gripping the steering wheel. The officer from the second car, seeing his movement, shouted again, and for a split second, Mr. A. was certain he was going to be shot. He remembers the blinding white of the spotlight, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth, the sound of his own heartbeat drowning out the sirens. He was ordered out of his car, forced to his knees, and handcuffed. It took several minutes for the officers to realize he was a bystander, not a threat. They uncuffed him with a curt apology and returned to the arrest. Mr. A. drove home shaking, the taste of copper still on his tongue.

In the weeks that followed, he could not stop replaying the moment the officer's gun pointed at his chest. The cockpit, once his sanctuary of order and control, became a cage. On final approach, he would suddenly see the red and blue strobes of police lights instead of runway lights. The crackle of the radio would sound like a shouted command. He began to avoid driving at night, taking long, circuitous routes to the airport to bypass any police presence. He started flying only day shifts, a significant professional sacrifice that his union representative questioned.

His marriage, already strained, could not bear the weight of his silence. He would wake his wife with his thrashing in bed, dreaming of the cold pavement against his cheek. When she asked what was wrong, he could only say, "Nothing. It was just a traffic stop." He felt a deep, corrosive shame. He was a man trained to remain calm under pressure, to navigate storms and mechanical failures. But he could not navigate this memory. He began drinking more heavily, a beer after every flight to "unwind," then two, then a bottle of wine. His wife left six months ago. He does not blame her.

Now, he lives in a sterile apartment near the airport. He has been on medical leave for three weeks after a panic attack in the simulator. He was practicing a crosswind landing when the instructor, a large man with a gruff voice, tapped him on the shoulder. The tap became the shout of the officer. Mr. A. unbuckled his harness and walked out of the simulator, his hands shaking so badly he could not hold his coffee. His PCL-5 score is 79, a reflection of the near-constant state of hypervigilance he lives in. He scans every parking lot for police cruisers. He checks his rearview mirror obsessively. He has not slept more than four hours a night in months. He avoids the news, especially stories about police, because the sight of a uniform makes his stomach clench. He describes a persistent, hollow feeling, as if the core of his competence has been scooped out and replaced with a trembling, watchful dread. He is here not because he wants to talk, but because he cannot fly, and flying is the only thing he knows how to do.
